sections.h2: How is New Mexico organized for a home sale?
sections.html:
New Mexico has 33 counties, and almost every step of a house sale runs through the one where the property sits. The county clerk records the deed, the county treasurer collects the tax bill, and the district court handles foreclosure and most probate questions. The state is large and thinly settled, so the office you call in Hidalgo County has little in common with the one in Bernalillo County.

The counties vary a great deal in size. Los Alamos County covers 109 square miles, while Catron County covers 6,928. Harding County had 617 residents in the figures Wikipedia lists, and Bernalillo County had 667,601. County seats are not always the biggest town: Hobbs is in Lea County, whose seat is Lovington, and Farmington is in San Juan County, whose seat is Aztec.

Our county sections below group each city page with the county guides we have written. If your town is not listed, the county clerk's office is still the right first call for recording questions.

  • Bernalillo, Sandoval and Santa Fe counties hold the metro areas around Albuquerque and Santa Fe.
  • Doña Ana, Otero and Eddy counties anchor the south.
  • Chaves, Curry and Lea counties cover the eastern plains and the oil country.
  • San Juan and McKinley counties sit in the northwest.

sections.h2: What does a cash sale of a house as-is mean in New Mexico?
sections.html:
A cash sale as-is means the buyer pays without a mortgage and takes the house in its current condition. You skip lender appraisals, repair requests and the weeks a loan approval can add. The sale still goes through a title search, a deed and a closing, just like any other.

New Mexico does not exempt an as-is sale from anything. Taxes owed on the property, a recorded judgment or an unpaid lien still show up on title and get paid from your proceeds at closing. Tell the buyer and the title company what you know about liens, tenants and open permits before you sign, because surprises usually surface during the title search anyway.

We buy houses in New Mexico in any condition, including homes with deferred repairs, tenants or probate questions. We do not promise a price before we see the property, and you are free to compare our offer with a listing, a different buyer or keeping the house.

sections.h2: How do property taxes work, and who do you call?
sections.html:
Property tax is a county matter. The county treasurer collects it, and under Section 7-38-38 of the state statutes, bills of $10 or more are payable in two equal installments, due November 10 and April 10 of the following year. No demand notice is required, so a missed date is the owner's problem.

The part that surprises sellers is the lien. Under Section 7-38-48, property taxes are a lien on real property from January 1 of the tax year, and that lien ranks ahead of any other interest in the property, perfected or unperfected. It also continues even while a protest or other tax dispute is pending. A buyer's title company will want it cleared or paid from proceeds.

ItemWhat the statute saysWho to call
Tax paymentsTwo equal installments, November 10 and April 10 (7-38-38)County treasurer
Tax lienFirst lien from January 1 of the tax year (7-38-48)County treasurer
Recording a deed$25 per document, plus $25 for each extra block of ten index entries (14-8-15)County clerk
Homestead protection from judgment creditors$150,000, or $300,000 in a recent-widow case (42-10-9)An attorney
Foreclosure redemptionNine months from the date of sale in a district court foreclosure (39-5-18)The district court clerk

We have written county guides for several areas. Start with the New Mexico property tax guide for state rules, then use the county sections below to find your treasurer and assessor.

sections.h2: How much does it cost to record a deed?
sections.html:
The statutory base fee is $25 per document. Section 14-8-15 tells the county clerk to collect $25 for each document recorded, and another $25 for each additional block of ten or fewer entries when a document has more than ten entries in the county recording index. The clerk may not accept a document until the fee is paid.

Of each $25 fee, $18 goes to the county general fund and the rest to the clerk's recording fund. Electronic filing services can add their own convenience fees, so ask the clerk what a given filing will cost.

Our guide on the Bernalillo County clerk covers recording in the state's largest county, and the quitclaim deed page explains what that form does and does not promise. If you want to know whether any transfer tax applies to your sale, ask the county clerk or your title company, since this page does not cover it.

sections.h2: How does foreclosure work, and how long can an owner redeem?
sections.html:
Most New Mexico mortgage foreclosures run through the district court, and the owner keeps a right to buy the house back after the sale. Section 39-5-18 gives the former owner nine months from the date of sale to redeem. The redeeming person pays the sale price, interest at ten percent a year, and taxes and prior lien payments the purchaser made. Redemption is done either by paying the purchaser or by petitioning the court and depositing the cash with the clerk.

Two details matter. The statute says the nine months can be modified under Section 39-5-19, so a loan document may shorten it. And a trustee's sale under a deed of trust is a different path, governed by the Deed of Trust Act. Which one applies to your loan depends on the paperwork, so ask a New Mexico foreclosure attorney or the lender.

If you are behind and want out before a sale, selling first usually leaves more for you than a forced sale. The tax deed and tax lien sales page covers the property tax version of this problem.

  • Gather the notice, the loan statements and the deed.
  • Ask the lender for a payoff figure in writing.
  • Contact a housing counselor or attorney early.
  • Request a closing date that falls before any sale date.

sections.h2: What happens to an inherited house in New Mexico?
sections.html:
Probate is needed when a house is titled in the dead owner's name. The New Mexico Courts self-help guide says probate is required for titled property such as real estate, and not required for real estate held in joint tenancy or with a recorded transfer on death deed.

A probate case is filed in the county where the person lived at death. The current probate court filing fee on that guide is $30, and a case can be filed between 5 days and 3 years after the death. Some cases must go to district court instead, and the probate court will say so.

Until a personal representative has authority, nobody can sell for the estate. Gather the death certificate, any will and the deed. Our pages on the probate process, the transfer on death deed and estate and inheritance tax go further.

sections.h2: Does the homestead exemption affect a sale?
sections.html:
The homestead exemption protects equity from judgment creditors. It does not cancel a mortgage or a tax lien. Under Section 42-10-9, a person has a homestead exemption in the home that is their primary residence, shielded from attachment, execution or foreclosure by a judgment creditor, and from receivers, bankruptcy trustees and probate administrators. The amount is $150,000, or $300,000 if the claimant's spouse died within two years and could have claimed it.

For a seller, the practical point is that the exemption limits what a creditor can collect, but a recorded judgment can still appear on title and get in the way of closing. Our homestead exemption guide explains the details. Talk to an attorney if a creditor is pursuing you.

sections.h2: What if the house has tenants?
sections.html:
A tenant's lease does not disappear because you decide to sell. Under the Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act, Section 47-8-33, an owner who wants to end a lease for a first material breach must deliver a written notice that names the dates and facts of the breach and states the rental agreement will end no sooner than seven days after receipt if the breach is not remedied in seven days. A second breach within six months follows a separate notice rule in the same section.

That is one route among several, and it does not cover every lease situation. We buy houses with tenants in place, which can spare you the move-out timeline. Our landlord and tenant guide explains what a rental sale involves.

  • Keep the lease and the rent ledger together.
  • Collect the deposit records before closing.
  • Give notices in writing and keep copies.

faqs.q: How many counties does New Mexico have?
faqs.a: New Mexico has 33 counties. Each has a county clerk who records deeds and a county treasurer who collects property tax.

faqs.q: When are New Mexico property taxes due?
faqs.a: Bills of $10 or more are due in two equal installments, November 10 and April 10 of the next year, under Section 7-38-38.

faqs.q: Do unpaid property taxes affect a sale?
faqs.a: Yes. Taxes are a first lien from January 1 of the tax year, so they are paid from proceeds at closing.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed?
faqs.a: The statutory base fee is $25 per document, with extra $25 charges for documents with more than ten index entries. Ask your county clerk for the current total.

faqs.q: How long can a foreclosed owner redeem?
faqs.a: In a district court foreclosure, nine months from the date of sale, though the period can be modified. Trustee's sales follow the Deed of Trust Act.

faqs.q: Do I need probate to sell an inherited house?
faqs.a: Usually, if the house is titled in the decedent's name. Joint tenancy or a recorded transfer on death deed avoids probate.

faqs.q: What is the New Mexico homestead exemption?
faqs.a: It is $150,000 of protection for a primary residence against judgment creditors, or $300,000 in a recent-widow case.

faqs.q: Will you buy a house with tenants or repairs?
faqs.a: Yes, we buy houses in any condition, including rentals and inherited homes. Call or text for details.
